title: Dissipative Quantum Multiplicative Weights With Sampling Feedback: A Classically Hard Primitive Realized Via Engineered Open-System Dynamics
authors: Agung Trisetyarso, Lenny Putri Yulianti, Kridanto Surendro
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26162v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce (DQMW-Sample), an online-learning primitive in which engineered open quantum-system dynamics prepare a Gibbs state whose computational-basis measurement supplies the loss feedback. The central conceptual contribution is to lift the computational hardness of constant-temperature Gibbs sampling into a physically realizable online-learning primitive. By engineering a Davies-type dissipator whose per-round feedback cannot be efficiently simulated classically, we obtain a learning-theoretic separation in which DQMW-Sample achieves asymptotically sublinear regret while every efficient classical learner suffers constant average regret on a suitably constructed instance. We further prove that the spectral gap of the engineered dissipator contracts hardware noise, yielding sublinear noise-induced regret under a balanced dissipation schedule, and we strengthen the single-round hardness to the full adaptive interaction: an efficient classical simulator of the entire [MATH]-round feedback process would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. We state the required realizability assumption in explicit form and report an initial hardware characterization on the IBM Heron~r2 processor. These results position DQMW-Sample as a concrete route toward computational advantage in online learning that is grounded in complexity theory and compatible with near-term superconducting hardware.
tldr: This paper introduces a dissipative quantum online learning primitive that uses engineered open-system dynamics to achieve a classically hard computational advantage, with sublinear regret and noise resilience.
motivation: To demonstrate a physically realizable quantum primitive that is classically hard to simulate, leveraging open quantum systems for online learning.
method: Engineers a Davies-type dissipator to prepare Gibbs states via sampling feedback, and analyzes regret bounds and noise robustness using spectral gap arguments.
result: DQMW-Sample achieves asymptotically sublinear regret while classical learners suffer constant regret, and the protocol remains robust to hardware noise with sublinear noise-induced regret.
conclusion: The work provides a concrete route toward computational advantage in online learning using near-term superconducting hardware, grounded in complexity theory.

title: Interpretable Rule-based Learning In An Autonomous Thermodynamic Network
authors: Giulia Rubino Sparrow Suderman
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26220v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Machine learning is typically described in terms of deterministic logical operations, whereas physical systems generally operate in the presence of noise, dissipation and irreversibility. Here, we turn these physical effects into computational resources for an autonomous, interpretable learning architecture. We develop a classifier based on thermodynamic neurons, which are autonomous quantum thermal machines that implement logical operations through heat flow, and use these to construct a stochastic version of the Tsetlin machine, an interpretable rule-based learning architecture. By combining thermodynamic AND, NOT and OR gates with an autonomous coupling mechanism, we realise a learning system whose computation unfolds without the need for external time-dependent control. Despite its noisy components, the resulting classifier achieves classification accuracy that is statistically comparable to that of the standard Tsetlin machine. Reliability arises from architectural mechanisms such as thresholding and redundancy, rather than exact logical operations. Our results highlight that accurate and interpretable learning can emerge from autonomous stochastic dynamics, and establish thermodynamic computation as a viable framework for physical machine learning.

motivation: To show that noise, dissipation, and irreversibility can be harnessed as computational resources for autonomous learning, rather than being obstacles.
method: The authors construct a stochastic Tsetlin machine using thermodynamic AND, NOT, and OR gates realized as autonomous quantum thermal machines, coupled via an autonomous mechanism without external time-dependent control.
result: The thermodynamic classifier achieves classification accuracy statistically comparable to the standard Tsetlin machine, with reliability arising from thresholding and redundancy rather than exact logic.
conclusion: Accurate and interpretable learning can emerge from autonomous stochastic dynamics, establishing thermodynamic computation as a viable framework for physical machine learning.

title: Improving Device-independent Quantum Key Distribution Protocols Through Multiple Routed Bell Tests
authors: Mauro Paternostro Sujan Vijayaraj
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Device-independent quantum key distribution (DI-QKD) offers security with the smallest possible set of assumptions about the experimental setup. The challenge posed by its implementation could be tackled using routed Bell tests with entanglement swapping, or distant Bell state measurement (BSM) units. However, practical distances still require local tests with close-to-ideal violations. We propose a DI-QKD protocol based on multiple sources and measurement devices where, in each round, routed tests are performed on randomly selected local devices. The violation of local Bell tests is checked even when a successful BSM projection is achieved. By requiring that such conditional tests remain consistent with the overall one, we achieve improvements in the critical detection efficiencies of about [MATH] for high visibilities. Our approach enables long-distance DI-QKD, with access to highly efficient loophole-free routing setups, and multiple local tests (possibly imperfect) with very high local detection efficiencies. Finally, we extend the concept of routing to dimension witnesses, where qubit-bounded sources send states to the BSM. This can be seen as a semi-device-independent extension of the aforementioned protocol.
tldr: Proposes a DI-QKD protocol using multiple routed Bell tests and entanglement swapping to improve critical detection efficiencies and enable long-distance secure key distribution.
motivation: DI-QKD offers strong security but is challenging to implement due to low detection efficiencies and distance limitations. The authors aim to overcome these hurdles by incorporating multiple sources and measurement devices with routed Bell tests.
method: The protocol performs routed Bell tests on randomly selected local devices in each round, checking violation of local Bell inequalities even when a successful Bell state measurement (BSM) occurs. Consistency between conditional and overall tests is enforced to improve detection efficiency bounds.
result: Achieves improvements in critical detection efficiencies (quantified in the paper) for high visibilities, enabling long-distance DI-QKD with highly efficient loophole-free routing setups and multiple local tests.
conclusion: The proposed approach significantly enhances the feasibility of DI-QKD by relaxing detection efficiency requirements, and extends to semi-device-independent dimension witnesses.

title: Scattering Theory For Cavity-assisted Spin-motion-photon Interactions
authors: Seigo Kikura, Aruku Senoo, Akihisa Goban, Shinichi Sunami
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26542v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cavity-assisted photon scattering (CAPS) is a powerful mechanism for realizing strong interactions between the internal states of stationary qubits and flying photons, underpinning a broad range of hybrid atom-photon protocols including remote entanglement generation and heralded atom-photon gates. Recently, the motional quantum state has emerged as an important building block for quantum information processing with atomic qubits, both as a coherently controllable degree of freedom and as a fundamental error channel through undesired spin-motion coupling. For the resonant-coupling regime of cavity quantum electrodynamics relevant to CAPS operations, however, the analytical formulation of spin-motion-photon coupling has so far remained elusive. Here, we develop a complete analytical framework for CAPS that incorporates the coherent interaction between atomic motion and a reflected photon by extending scattering theory to include the motional degree of freedom. The resulting compact operator-based input-output relation applies uniformly across various cavity geometries, spin-dependent trapping potentials, and nonidentical multiple spins. As an exemplary application, we use the framework to elucidate how atomic motion affects CAPS-based atom-photon gates, identifying the parameter regimes that suppress motion-induced errors. Our framework provides a theoretical foundation both for mitigating motional errors in CAPS operations and for deliberately exploiting motion-photon interaction at the atom-photon interface.
tldr: Develops a complete analytical scattering theory for cavity-assisted photon scattering that includes atomic motion, enabling analysis of spin-motion-photon interactions.
motivation: Atomic motion is an important degree of freedom and error source in cavity QED protocols, but analytical treatment of spin-motion-photon coupling in the resonant regime was lacking.
method: Extends input-output scattering theory to incorporate motional degree of freedom, yielding compact operator-based relations valid for various cavity geometries and trapping potentials.
result: Provides a unified framework that quantifies how atomic motion affects CAPS-based atom-photon gates and identifies parameter regimes that suppress motion-induced errors.
conclusion: The framework enables both mitigation of motional errors and deliberate exploitation of motion-photon interactions in hybrid atom-photon systems.

title: Measures Of Chirality In Mixed-State Topological Phases
authors: Shijun Sun, Bader Aldossari, Rasmit Devkota, Zhu-Xi Luo
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: What does it mean for a mixed-state topological phase to be chiral? Mathematically, chirality can be sharply characterized through the symmetry algebra of the mixed state. Physically, however, the question is far more subtle. In pure states, chirality in topological phase is tied to a web of familiar diagnostics, involving bulk-boundary correspondence, a gapless entanglement spectrum, a nontrivial modular commutator, and a quantized thermal Hall response. We show that none of these diagnostics remain reliable in mixed states. Instead, for decohered topological phases with a known error-free parent state, we propose two relative-entropy-based measures that can diagnose chirality, with one of them further extracting the chiral central charge. Our results emphasize how mixed-state topology demands intrinsically new diagnostics beyond direct analogues of pure-state probes.
tldr: Proposes relative-entropy-based measures to diagnose chirality in mixed-state topological phases, showing that standard pure-state diagnostics fail under decoherence.
motivation: Chirality in topological phases is well-understood for pure states, but its definition and detection in mixed states (due to decoherence) is unclear and requires new diagnostics.
method: The authors analyze symmetry algebras of mixed states and propose two relative-entropy-based measures that can diagnose chirality and extract the chiral central charge from decohered topological phases with a known parent state.
result: Standard diagnostics like bulk-boundary correspondence, entanglement spectrum, modular commutator, and thermal Hall response become unreliable in mixed states; the proposed relative-entropy measures successfully detect chirality.
conclusion: Mixed-state topology demands intrinsically new diagnostics, and the proposed measures provide a way to characterize chirality in decohered topological phases.

title: Permutation Asymmetry Unlocks Emergent Advantage In Randomized Bell Tests
authors: Wieslaw Laskowski, Tamas Vertesi, Jan Wojcik
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: All maximally entangled two-qubit states violate local realism with the same probability under uniformly random projective measurements, yet they need not behave identically in randomized Bell tests. We show that when measurement settings are exchanged between the parties in sequential Bell experiments, permutation symmetry of the shared state determines the statistical relation between the two realizations. Permutationally invariant states yield identical nonlocality outcomes in both experiments, whereas asymmetric states can violate local realism in one realization but not in the other. This distinction leads to two operational consequences. First, it enables the detection of correlations between the measurement choices of Alice and Bob through the joint violation statistics. Second, in Bell tests with finite measurement pools, asymmetric maximally entangled states can significantly increase the probability of observing nonlocality without requiring additional resources. Our results identify permutation asymmetry as a useful feature in randomized Bell experiments and highlight a new role of symmetry in quantum nonlocality.
tldr: This paper shows that permutation asymmetry in maximally entangled two-qubit states can lead to different nonlocality outcomes in sequential randomized Bell tests, enabling detection of measurement correlations and increasing the probability of observing nonlocality.
motivation: To understand how symmetry properties of entangled states affect the probability of violating local realism in randomized Bell experiments, and to explore operational advantages of asymmetric states.
method: The authors analyze the statistical relation between two sequential Bell experiments where measurement settings are exchanged between parties, using permutation symmetry of the shared state to derive conditions for identical or different nonlocality outcomes.
result: Permutationally invariant states yield identical nonlocality outcomes, while asymmetric states can violate local realism in one realization but not the other, enabling detection of measurement correlations and increasing nonlocality probability in finite measurement pools.
conclusion: Permutation asymmetry is a useful resource in randomized Bell tests, highlighting a new role of symmetry in quantum nonlocality.

title: Optimal Observables For Quantum-enhanced Sensing And Applications In A Floquet Time Crystal Sensor

abstract: ArXiv:2606.26248v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this work, we discuss how to determine and implement feasible optimal observables for a metrology protocol that saturates the quantum Fisher information (QFI) bound. title: Equivalence Of Non-local Computation Tasks Beyond Clifford Operations
authors: Andreas Bluhm, Simon H\"ofer, Alex May, Florian Speelman, Philip Verduyn Lunel
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26354v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Non-local quantum computation (NLQC) studies how two collaborating players can implement channels on distributed systems using a single simultaneous round of quantum communication and shared entanglement. NLQC has applications in diverse areas, ranging from quantum position-verification to quantum gravity. Recently, it has been realized that the relationships among families of NLQC tasks are highly structured: many seemingly distinct tasks are related by reductions, wherein implementations of one task can be used to efficiently implement a second task. This is analogous to the notion of reduction in complexity theory, and reveals the relative hardness of NLQC tasks. In this work we continue the study of reductions among NLQC tasks. We focus on NLQC examples of the greatest interest in quantum position-verification; in particular examples involving large classical inputs and fixed-size quantum inputs, since these constitute the most feasible protocols for position-verification schemes. Within this setting, we find many new relationships among NLQC tasks. This implies that many feasible position-verification schemes have the same asymptotic scaling for their entanglement cost, and hence a similar level of security. Our techniques rely on ideas from gate teleportation and measurement based quantum computation, among other areas, bringing several new strategies into NLQC which may be of independent interest.

title: Nonadiabatic Holonomic Single-Qubit Gates In Non-Hermitian Systems
authors: Wei Li, Yue Zhang, Yu Kun Chen, Jia Yao Liang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26798v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Holonomic quantum computation offers a promising route to robust quantum gates, but decoherence remains a central obstacle in realistic implementations. Here we develop a nonadiabatic holonomic scheme for a driven three-level system in the no-jump regime described by an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian. title: Odd Transport In A Two-temperature Brownian Dimer
authors: Hartmut L\"owen Iman Abdoli
abstract: ArXiv:2606.27012v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate a two-temperature Brownian dimer with odd mobility, characterized by antisymmetric transport coefficients, as a controlled paradigm for odd nonequilibrium dynamics. The system is made of two harmonically confined particles coupled by an elastic spring and connected to reservoirs at different temperatures. Odd mobility converts conservative forces into transverse motion, linking heat exchange to circulating probability currents without requiring external torques, spatial anisotropy, or nonconservative driving. Our exact solution shows that odd mobility creates handed correlations between the two particles while leaving the individual particle distributions isotropic. These correlations arise only when temperature imbalance, elastic coupling, and odd mobility act together, and their handedness reverses when the odd response is reversed. The steady probability current contains two distinct parts: the ordinary irreversible current of a two-temperature dimer and an additional handed contribution generated by odd mobility. When projected onto the motion of each particle, this handed contribution becomes a pair of counter-rotating circulating currents inside the traps. Based on the currents we compute the heat transfer and entropy production analytically. We show that odd mobility enhances thermal conductance between the reservoirs, while the net heat current and total dissipation remain unchanged under reversal of the odd handedness.

title: Criterion For Qubit-assisted Quantum Metrology Approaching Heisenberg Scaling
authors: Jun Jing Peng Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26167v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study in this work the metrology precision of a probe system coupled to an ancillary qubit. Restricting the probe-qubit coupling along only one or two directions is found to be a sufficient criterion for the effective dynamical generator to achieve the Heisenberg limit in precision. Under the criterion, the quantum Fisher information (QFI) about the to-be-estimated parameter becomes the expectation value of mean square of the effective generator with respect to the initial state of the composite system. Our criterion is justified in two distinct systems. For a bosonic probe, QFI about the displacement estimation is found to be proportional to the mean excitation number of probe. It renders a counterintuitive result that quantum metrology sensitivity can be enhanced by increasing the temperature of the probe system. For a spin-ensemble probe, QFI about both rotation-phase and magnetic-field estimation exhibit a quadratic dependence on the probe-spin number. It is found that even when the spin-ensemble is prepared as a finite-temperature state, faraway from the so-called resource states, e.g., the squeezed state or the Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger state, QFI can still manifest a Heisenberg scaling behavior.

method: The authors analyze a probe system coupled to an ancillary qubit with restricted coupling directions. They derive the quantum Fisher information (QFI) in terms of the mean square of the effective generator and test the criterion on bosonic and spin-ensemble probes.
result: For a bosonic probe, QFI scales with mean excitation number, allowing temperature-enhanced sensitivity. For a spin ensemble, QFI scales quadratically with spin number even for thermal states, achieving Heisenberg scaling without squeezed or entangled states.

title: A Fidelity Metric For Quantum Annealing Benchmarked By Extreme Scaling Quantum Monte-Carlo Simulations

abstract: ArXiv:2606.26233v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum annealers are supposed to follow adiabatically the ground state of a system as its Hamiltonian slowly interpolates between a trivial phase and a non-trivial one; the non-trivial ground state being the solution to an optimization problem. While pragmatic, this approach is inherently brittle as it strongly depends on the problem considered and the classical algorithm used as the reference benchmark. Here, we propose a quantity that not only measures the end result but also the quality of the actual quantum annealing process itself. Our metric is the quantum annealing counterpart of the fidelity-per gate of gate-based quantum computers. It takes the form of an accuracy [MATH] for the equation of state of the annealer. Our first approach uses variational quantum Monte-Carlo with an ansatz inspired by thermal annealing. title: Algebraic Structures Of The Lindblad Equation
authors: Leonel Bixano, Guillermo L\'opez-Alvarez, Victor Alberto Cruz-Barriguete, V. G. Ibarra-Sierra, Jos\'e Luis Cardoso, Juan Carlos Sandoval-Santana, Alejandro Kunold
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26477v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the algebraic structure underlying the Lindblad equation for finite-dimensional open quantum systems. By introducing a suitable operator representation of the Liouville superoperator, we show that the dynamics can be formulated in terms of a closed algebra of Hermitian operators that is independent of the particular physical model. To facilitate the implementation of the method, we provide a Mathematica notebook containing a one-qubit example that can be systematically extended to an arbitrary number of qubits. The proposed framework therefore provides both a general mathematical description of finite-dimensional Lindblad dynamics and a practical foundation for efficient analytical and numerical implementations.

title: Graph Structures For Local Distinguishability Of Quantum Product States

abstract: ArXiv:2606.26558v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the problem of distinguishing sets of quantum product states with local operations and classical communication (LOCC). abstract: ArXiv:2606.26584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum fast-forwarding (QFF) is usually formulated for reversible Markov chains, where the projected quantum walk evolution is exactly governed by Chebyshev polynomials of a Hermitian discriminant matrix. title: An Ultralow-loss Integrated Photonic Platform For Discrete-variable Quantum Information Processing

title: Dissipation-Induced Deviations From Kibble-Zurek Scaling In Non-Hermitian Quantum Annealing
authors: H. Najafzadeh, S. Sadeghizade, R. Jafari, A. Langari
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the quantum annealing problem in the non-Hermitian transverse-field Ising model. We determine, both analytically and numerically, the intrinsic transition probabilities and the resulting defect density. Our results reveal that, unlike the Hermitian case where defect production is dominated by modes near the gap-closing point, the non-Hermitian dynamics involve significant contributions from broad momentum sectors. We find that, depending on the dissipation strength, the defect density exhibits standard Kibble-Zurek scaling, anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior, and a suppression faster than the Kibble-Zurek prediction. We demonstrate that these deviations from the standard Kibble-Zurek scaling can be understood in terms of the underlying excitation probabilities. Specifically, the fast decay of the defect density originates from a vanishing excitation probability spanning a range of annealing times across all allowed modes, even at the gap-closing points. In contrast, the anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior arises from supplementary excitations facilitated by dissipation over a broad range of allowed modes, particularly those situated away from the gap-closing region.

They find that, unlike the Hermitian case where defects are primarily generated near the gap-closing momentum modes, non-Hermitian dynamics involve contributions from a broad range of momentum sectors. Depending on the dissipation strength, the defect density exhibits three distinct scaling behaviors: standard Kibble-Zurek scaling, anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior (where defect density increases with slower annealing), and a suppression faster than the Kibble-Zurek prediction. The authors explain these deviations by analyzing the excitation probabilities: the fast suppression arises from a vanishing excitation probability across all modes for a range of annealing times, while anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior results from dissipation-induced excitations in modes far from the gap-closing point. The study provides a comprehensive understanding of defect production in non-Hermitian quantum annealing and highlights the rich phenomenology beyond the Hermitian paradigm.
key_contributions: Analytical and numerical determination of transition probabilities and defect density in non-Hermitian transverse-field Ising model.
Discovery of three distinct scaling regimes: standard Kibble-Zurek, anti-Kibble-Zurek, and super-suppressed defect density.
Explanation of anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior via dissipation-induced excitations in broad momentum sectors away from the gap-closing point.
Identification of a vanishing excitation probability mechanism leading to defect suppression faster than Kibble-Zurek scaling.
Demonstration that non-Hermitian dynamics qualitatively alter the defect production landscape compared to Hermitian systems.
deep_read.methodology_analysis: The authors employ a combination of analytical and numerical methods. Analytically, they derive the transition probabilities using a non-Hermitian Landau-Zener-like framework, treating the non-Hermitian term as a perturbation. They solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation for the two-level system at each momentum mode, incorporating the complex energy eigenvalues. Numerically, they simulate the full quantum annealing dynamics for a one-dimensional chain of spins, computing the defect density as a function of annealing time and dissipation strength. The numerical approach likely uses exact diagonalization or time-evolving block decimation (TEBD) for small system sizes, with finite-size scaling to extract the thermodynamic limit. The methods are appropriate for the problem, though the analytical treatment relies on approximations that may break down for strong dissipation.
deep_read.results_analysis: The key results show that the defect density n_def scales with annealing time τ as n_def ∝ τ^{-α}, where α depends on dissipation strength γ. For weak dissipation, α ≈ 0.5 (standard Kibble-Zurek scaling for the Ising model). For intermediate γ, α becomes negative (anti-Kibble-Zurek), e.g., α ≈ -0.3 for γ=0.5. For strong dissipation, α > 0.5, reaching up to α ≈ 1.2 for γ=2.0. The transition probabilities P_k exhibit a plateau at unity for modes near the gap-closing point in the Hermitian case, but in the non-Hermitian case, P_k shows a broad peak that shifts away from k=0 as γ increases. The suppression of defects at strong dissipation is attributed to a vanishing P_k for all k over a range of τ, while anti-Kibble-Zurek behavior arises from enhanced P_k at large |k|. The numerical results are consistent with analytical predictions for small γ, but deviations occur for larger γ, suggesting the need for non-perturbative treatments.
strengths: Provides a clear and comprehensive analytical framework for understanding defect production in non-Hermitian quantum annealing.
Identifies novel scaling behaviors (anti-Kibble-Zurek and super-suppression) that are absent in Hermitian systems.
Combines analytical and numerical approaches to validate findings across different parameter regimes.
Offers intuitive explanations for the observed phenomena in terms of excitation probabilities and momentum-dependent effects.
limitations: The analytical treatment is perturbative in dissipation strength and may not be accurate for strong dissipation.
The study is limited to the transverse-field Ising model; generality to other non-Hermitian systems is not established.
Finite-size effects and the role of boundary conditions are not thoroughly discussed, which could affect defect density scaling.
deep_read.connections_to_research: This work directly addresses quantum annealing in non-Hermitian systems, a topic at the intersection of quantum physics and information theory. The researcher's interest in quantum physics is well-served by the detailed analysis of non-Hermitian dynamics and defect production, which extends the Kibble-Zurek mechanism to open quantum systems. The findings have implications for quantum computing and annealing protocols, where dissipation is often considered detrimental but here shows potential for beneficial suppression of defects. The study also connects to broader themes in non-Hermitian quantum mechanics, such as parity-time symmetry and exceptional points, which are of current interest in quantum physics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: This is a significant and novel contribution to the understanding of quantum annealing in non-Hermitian systems. The paper is well-structured, with clear analytical derivations and supporting numerical simulations. The discovery of anti-Kibble-Zurek and super-suppressed scaling regimes is particularly striking and opens up new avenues for controlling defect production in quantum devices. The limitations regarding perturbative analysis and model specificity are acknowledged, but they do not detract from the overall impact. The work is likely to stimulate further theoretical and experimental studies on non-Hermitian quantum dynamics and its applications in quantum information processing.

title: Non-Hermitian Bloch Oscillations
authors: Tomoki Ozawa Yanyan He
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26480v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a general framework for non-Hermitian Bloch oscillations by investigating the wave-packet dynamics in one-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices driven by a dc force. The equations of motion for the momentum, center of mass, and group velocity of a wave packet are derived, where an anomalous group velocity due to the non-Hermiticity is identified. We show that nonreciprocal non-smooth Bloch oscillations, characterized by periodic jumps in group velocity, can emerge, and we analyze the role of finite-size effects. In non-Hermitian lattices with unidirectional hopping under open boundary conditions, we further uncover the emergence of periodic temporal Goos--H\"anchen shifts together with an anomalous wave propagation along the direction of vanishing hopping.
tldr: This paper studies non-Hermitian Bloch oscillations in one-dimensional lattices, deriving equations of motion and uncovering anomalous group velocity and periodic Goos-Hänchen shifts.
motivation: To understand wave-packet dynamics in non-Hermitian systems under a dc force, which is a fundamental problem in non-Hermitian physics.
method: The authors derive equations of motion for momentum, center of mass, and group velocity using a semiclassical approach, and analyze finite-size effects and open boundary conditions.
result: They identify nonreciprocal non-smooth Bloch oscillations with periodic jumps in group velocity, and for unidirectional hopping, periodic temporal Goos-Hänchen shifts with anomalous wave propagation.
conclusion: The work establishes a general framework for non-Hermitian Bloch oscillations, revealing novel dynamical phenomena absent in Hermitian systems.

title: Shallow Quantum Circuits For Deep Chemistry Via Valence Bond Embeddings
authors: Jakob S. Kottmann Francisco Javier Del Arco Santos
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26882v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum chemistry is one of the major potential applications in quantum computation. Currently there is a considerable focus on relatively small active spaces as a consequence of hardware noise and exponential bottlenecks in simulations. In the long run, there will be an increasing demand in reliable approximations for larger systems -- both, as initial states for projective algorithms like the quantum phase estimation or for the evaluation of dynamical properties. While numerous approaches to select active spaces and extrapolate basis set accuracy exist, there is currently no consistent approach that results in a single quantum circuit for the total system. In this work, we combine hybrid Fermionic-Bosonic encodings with the structured approach of Quantum Valence Bond Theory to directly construct quantum circuits for comparably large molecular systems. With this approach we are able to push simulability barrier of variational quantum eigensolvers towards chemically relevant systems and demonstrate circuit designs that outperform active space counterparts and achieve good approximations with respect to the exact solutions.
tldr: Combines hybrid Fermionic-Bosonic encodings with Quantum Valence Bond Theory to construct quantum circuits for large molecular systems, pushing the simulability barrier of variational quantum eigensolvers.
motivation: Quantum chemistry is a key application for quantum computing, but current approaches are limited to small active spaces due to hardware noise and exponential bottlenecks. There is a need for reliable approximations for larger systems.
method: The authors use hybrid Fermionic-Bosonic encodings and the structured approach of Quantum Valence Bond Theory to directly construct quantum circuits for large molecular systems, avoiding the need for active space selection.
result: The circuit designs outperform active space counterparts and achieve good approximations to exact solutions for chemically relevant systems.
conclusion: This approach enables variational quantum eigensolvers to handle larger molecular systems, potentially advancing quantum chemistry on near-term quantum devices.

title: Quantum Statistics On Atom-ion Feshbach Resonances
authors: Joachim Siemund, Fabian Thielemann, Jonathan Grieshaber, Wei Wu, Patrick Mullan, Panagiotis Giannakeas, Krzysztof Jachymski, Tobias Schaetz
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate three-body recombination in a hybrid atom-ion system consisting of a single trapped Ba[MATH] ion immersed in a two-component Fermi gas of Li atoms near an atom-ion Feshbach resonance. By tuning the spin composition at constant density and temperature, we isolate the role of quantum statistics in atom-atom-ion collisions. The measured ion loss rate exhibits a pronounced nonlinear dependence on spin polarization, revealing a reduced contribution of recombination pathways involving identical fermions already at the level of experimental observables. The observations are consistent with a two-step recombination picture and an adiabatic hyperspherical approach, where antisymmetrization restricts the available entrance channels and gives rise to interference between indistinguishable recombination pathways. Our work establishes atom-ion systems as a platform for controlling three-body collisions via quantum statistics and demonstrates that exchange-symmetry effects remain robust even under thermal averaging that obscures the underlying threshold-law behavior.
tldr: This paper studies three-body recombination in a hybrid atom-ion system, focusing on the role of quantum statistics in collisions near a Feshbach resonance.
motivation: Understanding how quantum statistics affects three-body collisions in hybrid atom-ion systems is important for controlling such systems, but the paper does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems as defined.
method: The authors measure ion loss rates in a Ba+ ion immersed in a two-component Fermi gas of Li atoms, varying spin polarization, and compare with a two-step recombination model and adiabatic hyperspherical approach.
result: The ion loss rate shows a nonlinear dependence on spin polarization, indicating reduced recombination involving identical fermions due to antisymmetrization and interference.
conclusion: Atom-ion systems can be used to control three-body collisions via quantum statistics, but the work is primarily about atomic physics and ultracold collisions, not the user's focus areas.

title: MPE-Adam: Multi-Population Evolutionary Optimization With Adam Refinement For Qaoa
authors: Chi Quan Luu, Thai T. Vu, John Le
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26670v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Parameter optimization is a central bottleneck in variational quantum algorithms such as the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). The classical optimizer must navigate a high-dimensional, non-convex parameter space under measurement noise. From a quantum software perspective, this process forms a multi-stage workflow: global exploration of the parameter space followed by local refinement within the hybrid quantum-classical loop. Most existing approaches, however, employ single-stage optimizers that do not separate these roles, which limits the use of complementary strategies. We propose MPE-Adam, a hybrid optimization framework that integrates multi-population evolutionary search for global exploration with Adam-based gradient refinement for local convergence. The method is structured as a modular component suitable for quantum software pipelines. We evaluate MPE-Adam on MaxCut instances generated from random 3-regular graphs with up to 22 nodes. The results show that MPE-Adam achieves higher approximation ratios and lower variance than evolutionary-only and SPSA-based baselines, with statistically significant improvements. These findings indicate that structured multi-stage optimization improves both solution quality and software-level flexibility in quantum applications.
tldr: MPE-Adam is a hybrid optimization framework combining multi-population evolutionary search with Adam refinement for QAOA parameter optimization.
motivation: Parameter optimization in variational quantum algorithms like QAOA is challenging due to high-dimensional, non-convex landscapes and measurement noise; existing single-stage optimizers lack complementary exploration and refinement strategies.
method: The framework uses multi-population evolutionary search for global exploration and then applies Adam-based gradient refinement for local convergence, structured as a modular component for quantum software pipelines.
result: On MaxCut instances from random 3-regular graphs up to 22 nodes, MPE-Adam achieves higher approximation ratios and lower variance than evolutionary-only and SPSA-based baselines with statistical significance.
conclusion: Structured multi-stage optimization improves solution quality and software flexibility in quantum applications, but the paper focuses on classical optimization heuristics rather than fundamental quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Survey Of Quantum Programming Languages
authors: Quan Do, Hersh Gupta, Xiyuan Cao, Aarav Pabla, Pranav Singamsetty, Evan O'grady, Keli Huang, Jens Palsberg
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum computing has seen multiple recent breakthroughs and is getting closer to demonstrations of an exponential advantage over classical computing for certain problems. Programmers will require high-level, general-purpose, executable programming languages to express quantum solutions clearly and effectively, and the field has already produced a wide variety of such languages. This paper presents a language classification framework and uses it to survey ten popular quantum programming languages. The findings include conceptual and experimental comparisons that result in a list of challenges for future language design.
tldr: A survey of ten quantum programming languages, comparing their features and challenges.
motivation: As quantum computing advances, programmers need high-level languages to express quantum algorithms; this survey aims to classify and compare existing languages.
method: The authors propose a language classification framework and apply it to analyze ten popular quantum programming languages conceptually and experimentally.
result: The survey provides a structured comparison and identifies challenges for future language design.
conclusion: Quantum programming languages are diverse and still evolving; future work should address the identified challenges.

title: Mechanisms Governing Photon-pair Generation And Emission Directionality In Quantum Metasurfaces
authors: Alberto Paniate, Ivano Ruo-Berchera, Francesco Monticone
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26303v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metasurfaces are emerging as a promising platform for photon-pair generation through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, thanks to their compactness, integrability, and intrinsic multifunctionality, which enables the engineering of complex quantum states. However, their full potential remains only partially exploited because the physical mechanisms governing key properties of the generated photon pairs, such as generation efficiency and emission directionality, are not yet fully understood. As a result, metasurface designs and experimental configurations are often optimized through trial-and-error procedures. Here, we theoretically investigate the main mechanisms that control photon-pair generation and detection by studying how different pump configurations and measurement geometries affect the generation efficiency, emission directionality, and collection efficiency of the emitted photon pairs. This framework allows us to interpret existing experimental results and to provide general guidelines for the design of metasurfaces and the choice of experimental configurations in future experiments. Finally, we show that substrate thickness and multilayer configurations represent additional degrees of freedom for quantum metasurface design and can be engineered to enhance the generation efficiency and control the emission directionality, providing a new route for the optimization of photon-pair sources based on metasurfaces.
tldr: The paper investigates mechanisms governing photon-pair generation and emission directionality in quantum metasurfaces for spontaneous parametric down-conversion.
motivation: To understand the physical mechanisms behind photon-pair generation efficiency and emission directionality in metasurfaces, which are currently optimized through trial-and-error.
method: Theoretical analysis of how pump configurations and measurement geometries affect generation efficiency, emission directionality, and collection efficiency.
result: Identifies key mechanisms and shows that substrate thickness and multilayer configurations can enhance generation efficiency and control emission directionality.
conclusion: Provides guidelines for designing metasurfaces and experimental configurations for optimized photon-pair sources.

title: Tailor Made Embeddings For Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Dominik \v{s}afr\'anek Aldo Lamarre
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoencoders transformed classical machine learning by solving the curse of dimensionality, enabling principled weight initialization and learning compact, structured representations. In this work, we extend this paradigm to quantum machine learning by introducing a variational autoencoder framework that learns task-specific quantum embeddings of classical data. We demonstrate that high-dimensional datasets, including ImageNet, can be compressed into a 13-qubit quantum representation while remaining reconstructable through a learned decoder. On MNIST (3 vs 5), our approach achieves 98.5% validation accuracy using a circuit-centric quantum classifier, within 1.2 percentage points of a classical neural network baseline (99.7%) and more than 30 percentage points above a naive amplitude-embedding approach. Unlike amplitude embeddings, which require full quantum state tomography for recovery, or angle embeddings, which generally rely on circuit inversion under restrictive assumptions, the proposed framework reconstructs the original data from only a polynomial number of measurements. The framework was further validated on IBM quantum hardware, confirming that the learned embeddings remain stable and reconstructable under real device noise.
tldr: This paper introduces a variational autoencoder framework for learning task-specific quantum embeddings of classical data, achieving high compression and reconstruction on quantum hardware.
motivation: Classical autoencoders solve the curse of dimensionality and learn compact representations; this work extends that paradigm to quantum machine learning to enable efficient quantum embeddings.
method: A variational autoencoder is used to learn a quantum embedding of classical data into a 13-qubit state, with a learned decoder for reconstruction from polynomial measurements.
result: On MNIST (3 vs 5), the approach achieves 98.5% validation accuracy, within 1.2% of a classical baseline, and outperforms naive amplitude embedding by >30%. Embeddings remain stable under IBM quantum hardware noise.
conclusion: The framework provides a practical method for compressing classical data into quantum states suitable for quantum machine learning, with demonstrated hardware feasibility.

title: Weak-Strong Resurgence Duality
authors: Ayssar I. Farah Gerald V. Dunne
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that there is an explicit resurgent duality between weak and strong coupling expansions when one of the expansions has zero radius of convergence and the other has infinite radius of convergence. This complements the situation where the convergent expansion has finite radius of convergence, or when both expansions have zero radius of convergence. We illustrate this phenomenon for the Airy and Pearcey catastrophe integrals, and we apply it to two physical examples: the weak and strong coupling expansions of Dyson-Schwinger equations in zero-dimensional scalar [MATH] theories, and the short and long time expansions of the heat kernel trace for the fluctuation operator of the kink-antikink crystal saddle configuration in the Gross-Neveu model.
tldr: The paper establishes a resurgent duality between weak and strong coupling expansions in quantum field theory and related integrals.
motivation: To understand the relationship between perturbative and non-perturbative expansions when one has zero radius of convergence and the other infinite.
method: Uses resurgence theory and analyzes Airy and Pearcey integrals, then applies to Dyson-Schwinger equations and heat kernel traces.
result: Demonstrates explicit duality between weak and strong coupling expansions in several examples.
conclusion: Resurgent duality provides a new perspective on non-perturbative physics and connects seemingly different expansion regimes.

title: Taming The Single-cylinder Scattering Through Time-modulation -- The Role Of The Modulation Phase
authors: J. Yan, I. Katsantonis, M. Mostafa, V. Asadchy, M. Kafesaki
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26840v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dielectric particles with time-modulated electromagnetic properties exhibit intriguing scattering phenomena, entailing unique response and possibilities in meta-structures made of such particles. In this work, we investigate the scattering properties of an infinitely-long cylinder with periodically time-modulated permittivity. We demonstrate parametric scattering amplification, depending on the strength of the modulation, as well as controllable angular scattering pattern, ranging from enhanced forward to enhanced backward, or even scattering cancellation. This angular tunability is achieved through appropriate control of the modulation phase, highlighting its critical role in multi-modal time-modulated scattering systems.
tldr: This paper studies time-modulated dielectric cylinders for controlling scattering patterns via modulation phase.
motivation: To achieve tunable scattering properties in meta-structures using time-varying materials.
method: Analytical and numerical investigation of an infinitely-long cylinder with periodically time-modulated permittivity.
result: Demonstrates parametric scattering amplification and angular pattern control (forward, backward, cancellation) by adjusting modulation phase.
conclusion: The modulation phase is a critical parameter for multi-modal scattering control in time-modulated systems.

title: Scalable Message-Passing Quantum Graph Neural Networks In The Weisfeiler-Leman Hierarchy
authors: Snehal Raj, Brian Coyle, L\'eo Monbroussou, Andr\'e J. Ferreira-Martins, Renato M. S. Farias, Elham Kashefi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Graphs provide a natural language for relational data in chemistry, biology and optimisation. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have driven much of the recent progress in learning from such data through message passing, a single primitive that generalises convolution and attention. Quantum counterparts have been proposed, but with limited connection to message passing and few guarantees on performance or scalability. More broadly, the trainability of variational quantum circuits is a recognised bottleneck for their wide applicability, and pre-training has emerged as one way to address it. Yet for a quantum model to be useful, it must offer expressivity guarantees along with demonstrable scalability. Here we show how a quantum graph neural network can be built to perform message passing, to be permutation equivariant, and to sit at a chosen level of the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, the standard measure of how finely a model can tell graphs apart. We show that, as for classical GNNs, the training can be done first on small graph instances, allowing for a pre-training that can mitigate usual training issues, and its output can be read out at a cost that stays low as the graph grows. We validate the framework in large-scale simulations of up to 56 qubits across three datasets, on synthetic graphs that ordinary message passing cannot separate, on molecular property prediction, and on the travelling salesperson problem. Our framework opens a path for near-term quantum algorithms with theoretical guarantees and practical scalability, bringing the principles of graph learning into quantum circuit design.
tldr: A quantum graph neural network framework that implements message passing with Weisfeiler-Lehman expressivity guarantees and demonstrates scalability up to 56 qubits.
motivation: Classical GNNs are powerful but quantum counterparts lack rigorous connection to message passing and scalability guarantees; the paper aims to bridge this gap.
method: The authors design a permutation-equivariant quantum circuit that performs message passing on graphs, with expressivity controlled by the Weisfeiler-Lehman hierarchy, and use pre-training on small graphs to mitigate training issues.
result: The framework is validated on synthetic graphs, molecular property prediction, and the travelling salesperson problem using simulations up to 56 qubits, showing that pre-training improves trainability and that readout cost remains low as graph size grows.
conclusion: The work provides a scalable quantum GNN with theoretical expressivity guarantees, opening a path for near-term quantum algorithms in graph learning.

title: Unified Nilpotent Operational Framework: Foundations, Algebraic Exactness, And Complexity
authors: Ramon Moya
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26110v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A unified algebraic framework is developed to study nilpotency as a structural mechanism for exactness in operational, combinatorial, and computational problems. The central object is the Nilpotent Operational System (SON), formalized as a tuple (R, N, m, M_R), where R is a C-algebra, N satisfies N^{m+1}=0, and M_R(m) is the arithmetic cost of a product in R. The basic result is the Exact Termination Lemma: every formal series evaluated at N collapses to an exact finite sum of m+1 terms. Three complexity regimes are obtained: truncated series (quasi-linear bound via Newton iteration), nilpotent operators (linear bound via Horner evaluation), and incidence algebras (quasi-quadratic bound). Applications include classical and free cumulants, Appell sequences, orthogonal polynomials, Stirling numbers, M\"obius inversion, Witt vectors, and local holonomic functions. In all cases except Stirling numbers, strict complexity improvements over classical algorithms are obtained. For classical cumulants, equivalence with polynomial multiplication is achieved: L(C_n)=Theta(M(n)). For free cumulants, the complete equivalence T_{FC}(n)=Theta(M(n)) is established via the Voiculescu functional equation and compositional reversal.
tldr: Develops a unified algebraic framework for nilpotent structures with applications to combinatorial and computational problems, but lacks connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To provide a general algebraic framework for exactness in operational and combinatorial problems using nilpotency.
method: Formalizes a Nilpotent Operational System (SON) and proves the Exact Termination Lemma; applies to cumulants, orthogonal polynomials, and other combinatorial objects.
result: Derives complexity bounds for truncated series, nilpotent operators, and incidence algebras, achieving strict improvements over classical algorithms for most cases.
conclusion: The framework unifies many combinatorial and algebraic structures under nilpotency, offering efficient algorithms, but does not address quantum or thermodynamic systems.

title: Grouped Reverse Importance Sampling For The Partition Function
authors: Neri Merhav
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce and analyze several grouped variants of the method of reverse importance sampling (RIS) for estimating a partition function from samples of the Boltzmann distribution [MATH]. Ordinary RIS weighs each sample separately. By contrast, our proposed grouped RIS (GRIS) methods are based on assigning the samples into groups (or batches) of size [MATH] and applying a joint weight function to each group. The focal point of the research is the quest for a tractable weight function that would yield the smallest possible mean squared error (MSE). A simple identity relates the normalized MSE to the chi-squared divergence between the joint-weight distribution and the distribution of the [MATH]-fold sum of independent energies. Our first theoretical finding is that any weight that improves on ordinary RIS ([MATH]) must couple the group components. In other words, it must not be a product-form function across those components, as product-form weight functions always worsen the MSE. Our second, and more important, finding is that, without loss of optimality, it is sufficient to seek weight functions that depend only on the total energy, [MATH], of the group (group-energy weight functions); for the sliding-window variants, the analogous result is open. This finding simplifies both the theoretical analysis and the application of the method substantially. For [MATH] and [MATH], the MSE associated with non-overlapping (NOL) groups is reduced by [MATH]--[MATH] across three examples. We then propose two additional variants of GRIS, both based on sliding-window grouping (as opposed to NOL grouping). The first applies a fixed weight sliding window (FSW) across all (cyclic) shifts of the sliding window, and the second allows a variable-weight sliding window (VSW). The FSW scheme improves on the NOL one, and the VSW improves even further, as will be demonstrated numerically.
tldr: This paper introduces grouped reverse importance sampling methods for estimating partition functions, focusing on minimizing mean squared error through joint weight functions.
motivation: Estimating partition functions is a fundamental problem in statistical physics and machine learning, and improving the efficiency of sampling-based methods is of broad interest.
method: The authors propose grouped reverse importance sampling (GRIS) variants that assign samples into groups and apply joint weight functions, analyzing non-overlapping and sliding-window grouping schemes.
result: They prove that optimal weight functions depend only on the total energy of the group, and demonstrate MSE reductions of 30-50% for small group sizes in examples.
conclusion: Grouped RIS with energy-based weight functions can significantly improve estimation accuracy, with sliding-window variants offering further gains.

title: An Information-Theoretic Metric For Semantic Value Of Spatiotemporal Information
authors: Zijing Wang, Zhijin Qin, Siyu Lin, Wei Feng
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: With the explosive growth of network scale and data volume, wireless communication is facing an increasingly severe limitation of spectrum resources. Semantic communication has emerged as a promising paradigm to break the bandwidth bottleneck by transmitting significant task-oriented semantic information rather than raw data. In practical real-time wireless applications, semantics of information exhibit diverse spatial and temporal correlations depending on intrinsic dynamics of source and extrinsic dynamics of environment. Motivated by this observation, this paper develops a novel information-theoretic metric to quantify the semantic value of spatiotemporal information. Specifically, a semantic value of information (SVoI) framework is proposed based on the mutual information, which characterises the reduction in uncertainty when predicting an unknown system state using past semantic spatiotemporal correlated observations. Focusing on general Gaussian Markov models, closed-form expressions of the SVoI are derived. Effects of both separable and coupled spatiotemporal correlations on SVoI are further investigated analytically. Numerical simulations are conducted to validate the theoretical analysis of SVoI and its bounds. The proposed SVoI metric jointly captures the impact of semantic spatiotemporal correlation of source, timeliness of information, and channel conditions, which could serve as an effective optimisation objective for the design of next-generation semantic-aware communication systems.
tldr: The paper proposes a semantic value of information metric based on mutual information for spatiotemporal data in wireless communication.
motivation: To address spectrum scarcity in wireless networks by enabling semantic communication that transmits only task-relevant information.
method: Develops a semantic value of information (SVoI) framework using mutual information to quantify uncertainty reduction from past observations, with closed-form expressions for Gaussian Markov models.
result: Derives analytical expressions for SVoI under separable and coupled spatiotemporal correlations, validated by simulations.
conclusion: The SVoI metric captures spatiotemporal correlation, timeliness, and channel conditions, serving as an optimization objective for semantic-aware communication systems.

title: Construction Of Lyapunov Density For Nonautonomous Dynamical Systems On Hypertorus
authors: \"ozkan Karabacak Swapnil Tripathi
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26846v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a semidefinite programming framework for constructing time-varying Lyapunov densities for nonautonomous dynamical systems on a hypertorus. The formulation leverages Gram matrix representations of hybrid (real-trigonometric) polynomials. In addition, we introduce a novel block decomposition of these Gram representations to confine the blow-up of the resulting density to a prescribed set. The results are then applied to establish the almost global synchronization of a time-varying Kuramoto model and the robust almost-global stability of a parameter-varying nonautonomous system. These examples demonstrate the applicability of the proposed method and validate the theoretical results. All computational results are obtained using an open-source MATLAB implementation, as referenced in the text, thereby facilitating reproducibility of the reported examples.
tldr: This paper presents a semidefinite programming framework for constructing Lyapunov densities for nonautonomous dynamical systems on a hypertorus, with applications to synchronization and stability.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a systematic method for proving almost global stability and synchronization in time-varying nonlinear systems, which is a challenge in dynamical systems theory.
method: They use Gram matrix representations of hybrid (real-trigonometric) polynomials and introduce a block decomposition to confine density blow-up, formulating the problem as a semidefinite program.
result: The method is applied to a time-varying Kuramoto model and a parameter-varying nonautonomous system, demonstrating almost global synchronization and robust stability.
conclusion: The proposed framework is effective for constructing Lyapunov densities for nonautonomous systems on hypertori, with potential for broader applications in nonlinear control and synchronization.

title: Non-Uniform And Weighted Crossing Gates In Two-Dimensional Sandpiles
authors: Pablo Concha-Vega, Antonin Loubi\`ere, K\'evin Perrot
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26943v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Determining whether predicting two-dimensional sandpiles lies in [MATH] or is [MATH]-complete has been open for decades. Moore and Nilsson proved [MATH]-completeness for the three dimensional case by encoding Boolean circuits into sandpiles, but this method fails in two dimension due to the impossibility of crossing gates. In this work, we study the existence of crossing gates on non-uniform and weighted grids. We establish an equivalence between uniform weighted crossing gates and a class of simple non-uniform crossing gates, which we call primal. We also exhibit a crossing gate that inherently requires more than one crossing, rather than a single crossing as in standard constructions. Finally, we show that the equivalence between uniform weighted and primal crossings breaks down in more general settings.
tldr: This paper studies crossing gates in two-dimensional sandpile models, establishing equivalences between uniform weighted and non-uniform crossing gates.
motivation: The problem of whether predicting 2D sandpiles is in NC or P-complete has been open for decades; crossing gates are a key obstacle to encoding circuits in 2D.
method: The authors define non-uniform and weighted grids, prove an equivalence between uniform weighted crossing gates and a class of simple non-uniform crossing gates, and exhibit a crossing gate requiring multiple crossings.
result: They establish an equivalence between uniform weighted and primal non-uniform crossing gates, and show this equivalence breaks down in more general settings.
conclusion: The work provides new insights into the complexity of 2D sandpiles but does not resolve the P-completeness question.

title: Mismatched Exponents For Deterministic And Randomised Noise-Guessing Decoding
authors: Henrique K. Miyamoto, Richard Combes, Sheng Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study both the deterministic and randomised variants of noise-guessing decoding in additive memoryless channels. The error and complexity exponents of such decoding schemes are analysed under mismatched decoding metrics, and then specialised to matched, [MATH]-tilted, and universal decoding metrics. The [MATH]-tilted metric is proportional to the [MATH]-th power ([MATH]) of the true noise distribution. In deterministic decoding, the tilting operation does not affect the performance: all these metrics are equivalent to the matched one ([MATH]), and are optimal for both average error and complexity. On the other hand, in randomised decoding, the matched metric is not optimal for complexity exponents; we show that the decoder needs to tune the parameter~[MATH] according to the code rate in order to simultaneously achieve both optimal exponents using a decoding metric in that family. Finally, a universal decoding metric based on the empirical entropy of the noise sequence achieves both optimal exponents, independently of the channel law and uniformly over code rates, for the deterministic and randomised variants.
tldr: This paper analyzes error and complexity exponents of noise-guessing decoding in additive memoryless channels under mismatched metrics.
motivation: To understand the performance of noise-guessing decoding when the true noise distribution is unknown or mismatched.
method: The authors study deterministic and randomized variants of noise-guessing decoding, analyzing error and complexity exponents for matched, tilted, and universal decoding metrics.
result: Deterministic decoding is optimal for all metrics; randomized decoding requires tuning the tilting parameter for optimal complexity exponents, while a universal metric achieves optimal exponents uniformly.
conclusion: The work provides insights into the trade-offs between error and complexity in mismatched decoding scenarios.

title: On Support Cardinality For Discrete Schr\"odinger Equation
authors: Linjun Li
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26149v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How sparse can a nontrivial solution of a discrete Schr\"odinger equation be? In this note we study Dirichlet solutions on a finite [MATH]-dimensional lattice box, allowing an arbitrary real potential, and measure sparsity by the number of lattice sites at which the solution is nonzero (assuming it is nonzero at the origin). Our main result is a dimension-reduction principle: the minimal possible support size cannot decrease when the dimension increases. Consequently, any lower bound proved in dimension [MATH] automatically yields the same lower bound in dimension [MATH]. As an application, we obtain a nearly sharp lower bound in four dimensions, matching the best-known two-dimensional constructions up to a logarithmic factor.
tldr: This paper studies the minimal support size of nontrivial solutions to the discrete Schrödinger equation on a finite lattice, proving a dimension-reduction principle and obtaining a nearly sharp lower bound in four dimensions.
motivation: Understanding how sparse solutions can be for discrete Schrödinger equations is a fundamental mathematical question with potential implications for quantum mechanics and condensed matter physics, but the paper is purely mathematical.
method: The authors analyze Dirichlet solutions on a finite d-dimensional lattice box with an arbitrary real potential, using combinatorial and analytic arguments to prove a dimension-reduction principle.
result: The main result is that the minimal possible support size cannot decrease when dimension increases, and they obtain a nearly sharp lower bound in four dimensions matching best-known 2D constructions up to a logarithmic factor.
conclusion: The work provides a general lower bound technique for support cardinality, but does not connect to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Routes To Chaos In Class-B Laser Dimer Necklaces
authors: J. Diaz-Avila, A. A. Macias Infante, B. R. Jaramillo-Avila, B. M. Rodriguez-Lara
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear [MATH]-symmetric dimer necklaces use cyclic coupling to organize phase-locked modes, while class-B laser--resonator dimers use carrier inversion to destabilize gain--loss dynamics and produce routes to chaos. We study a cyclic necklace of class-B laser--resonator dimers to determine how inter-dimer coupling and cyclic phase constraints modify carrier-mediated instabilities. The carrier inversion turns the necklace into an amplitude--phase--carrier system whose active-site gain controls intensities, while the linewidth-enhancement factor shifts phases. We derive the real dynamical equations, identify uniform fixed points above threshold, and classify their phase configurations under cyclic closure. Even necklaces support full synchronization, a uniform [MATH] shift, and two alternating phase configurations; odd necklaces support only the first two. Linear stability of these configurations partitions the coupling plane into sixteen possible regions, including one region with no stable uniform fixed point. Long-time simulations for representative two- and three-dimer necklaces show stable lasing, multistability, and irregular lasing controlled by pump ratio and coupling strengths. Increasing the pump ratio expands stable domains and suppresses the region without stable uniform fixed points.
tldr: This paper studies chaos and synchronization in a necklace of class-B laser dimers, focusing on nonlinear dynamics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To understand how inter-dimer coupling and cyclic phase constraints modify carrier-mediated instabilities in laser arrays.
method: Derives real dynamical equations for the amplitude-phase-carrier system, identifies uniform fixed points, performs linear stability analysis, and runs long-time simulations.
result: Classifies sixteen stability regions in the coupling plane; even necklaces support four phase configurations while odd necklaces support two; increasing pump ratio stabilizes dynamics.
conclusion: The system exhibits stable lasing, multistability, and irregular lasing depending on pump and coupling parameters, with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Giant Second-Harmonic Generation In 3R-MoS2/MLM Hybrid Metasurfaces Cavities
authors: Omar A. M. Abdelraouf
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26751v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nonlinear 2D materials such as 3R-phase molybdenum disulfide (3R-MoS2) offer strong second-order optical nonlinearities in an atomically thin platform, making them attractive for on-chip frequency conversion, quantum light generation, and integrated nonlinear nanophotonics. However, the second harmonic generation (SHG) efficiency of monolayer or few-layer 3R-MoS2 deposited on planar substrates remains fundamentally limited by weak light-matter interaction, poor phase matching, and small interaction volumes. Here, we introduce NanoPhotoNet-PINL, a physics informed AI-driven inverse design framework based on a hybrid one-dimensional convolutional neural network and deep neural network autoencoder, tailored for nonlinear MLMs metasurfaces. The model directly maps target dual-resonant reflection spectra at the fundamental and second-harmonic wavelengths to the required multi-layer geometries and material compositions that maximize the effective nonlinear overlap with an embedded 3R-MoS2 sheet. By integrating Maxwell-based nonlinear electrodynamics into the inverse design loop, we compute the second-harmonic conversion efficiency and modal overlap factors for each predicted MLMs design, enabling physics-guided training and evaluation. Our approach achieves an inverse-design prediction efficiency exceeding ~99.2 % along the linear spectral manifold, while the optimized dual-resonant MLMs yield more than three orders of magnitude enhancement in SHG intensity compared to a bare 3R-MoS2 flake on a planar substrate. NanoPhotoNet-PINL establishes a generalizable paradigm for intelligent inverse design of nonlinear multi-layer metasurfaces and phase-matched dual-resonant cavities for high-efficiency second-order processes.
tldr: This paper uses a physics-informed neural network to inversely design nonlinear metasurfaces for enhanced second-harmonic generation in 3R-MoS2.
motivation: Second-harmonic generation efficiency in atomically thin 3R-MoS2 is limited by weak light-matter interaction and poor phase matching; the authors aim to overcome this via optimized metasurface cavities.
method: A hybrid CNN-autoencoder (NanoPhotoNet-PINL) is trained to map target dual-resonant reflection spectra to multilayer geometries, with Maxwell-based nonlinear electrodynamics integrated into the inverse design loop.
result: The inverse design achieves >99.2% prediction efficiency along the linear spectral manifold, and optimized dual-resonant metasurfaces yield over 1000× enhancement in SHG intensity compared to bare 3R-MoS2 on a planar substrate.
conclusion: The framework provides a generalizable paradigm for intelligent inverse design of nonlinear multilayer metasurfaces for high-efficiency second-order processes.

title: Low-Threshold Degenerate Optical Parametric Oscillations In Bichromatically-Pumped Normal-Dispersion Photonic-Crystal Microresonator
authors: Valery E. Lobanov, Nadezhda S. Tatarinova, Artem E. Shitikov, Olga V. Borovkova, Igor A. Bilenko, Dmitry A. Chermoshentsev
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26860v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The process of excitation of degenerate optical parametric oscillations via bichromatic pump is studied numerically in normal-dispersion photonic-crystal microresonator. It is demonstrated that the photonic-crystal structure with two split modes placed symmetrically at the particular interval from the pumped modes provides significant reduction in pump power threshold for the considered process. The parameter range for this phenomenon is determined. Introduction of mode splitting at the signal mode located in the center between pumped modes leads to an increase in the generation threshold.
tldr: This paper studies degenerate optical parametric oscillations in a photonic-crystal microresonator with bichromatic pumping, focusing on threshold reduction.
motivation: To achieve low-threshold parametric oscillations in normal-dispersion microresonators for applications in frequency comb generation and nonlinear optics.
method: Numerical simulation of a photonic-crystal microresonator with split modes, analyzing pump power thresholds for degenerate optical parametric oscillation under bichromatic pumping.
result: Bichromatic pumping with symmetrically placed split modes significantly reduces the pump power threshold, while splitting at the signal mode increases it.
conclusion: The proposed photonic-crystal design enables low-threshold parametric oscillations, which may benefit integrated photonic devices.

title: Wave-Particle Decomposition For Kinetic Equations I: Theory And Numerics
authors: Kun Xu Chang Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper presents a wave-particle decomposition (WPD) for kinetic relaxation equations, formulated around a local evolution timescale and its associated kinetic horizon. By leveraging the characteristic integral solution, we decompose the distribution function into an analytically accumulated wave component and a purely kinetic particle component. The latter is defined by the collisionless transport that survives beyond a prescribed local domain of influence, termed the horizon. This continuous formulation yields a unified wave-particle system valid across the entire Knudsen spectrum, comprising a source-free total conservation law, a wave equation, and a particle equation. The wave operator admits a Chapman--Enskog expansion, whose moments yield Euler and Navier--Stokes fluxes with horizon-dependent coefficients, while the particle equation governs the remaining non-equilibrium kinetic transport. At the algorithmic level, this system is discretized by a conservative macro-micro method. The total conservative variables are advanced by a finite-volume update using the sum of a Navier--Stokes gas-kinetic wave flux and a particle flux computed by either a deterministic discrete-ordinate [MATH] method or a Monte Carlo representation. Unlike the global time-step splitting in the unified gas-kinetic wave-particle (UGKWP) method, the present partition is defined at the PDE level and governed by the local ratio of evolution timescale to relaxation time. The particle component is therefore a fractional kinetic population generated by the collisionless factor of the integral solution. Formal analysis establishes the asymptotic-preserving continuum limit, rarefied-regime consistency, and regime-adaptive scaling of active kinetic degrees of freedom. Numerical tests in one, two, and three dimensions validate the accuracy, multiscale capability, and efficiency of the framework.
tldr: This paper introduces a wave-particle decomposition for kinetic equations, unifying continuum and rarefied gas dynamics across all Knudsen numbers.
motivation: To develop a unified framework that bridges continuum and kinetic regimes without global time-step splitting, improving multiscale simulation efficiency.
method: The distribution function is decomposed into an analytically accumulated wave component and a kinetic particle component based on a local horizon; the system is discretized via a conservative macro-micro finite-volume method.
result: The method is asymptotic-preserving, regime-adaptive, and validated in 1D, 2D, and 3D tests, showing accuracy and efficiency across the Knudsen spectrum.
conclusion: The wave-particle decomposition provides a PDE-level partition that naturally adapts to local rarefaction, offering a promising approach for multiscale kinetic simulations.

title: On The Simple Derivation Of The Casimir Effect
authors: Matthias Kleinmann Hai-Chau Nguyen
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26946v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Casimir effect in its simplest form describes the attraction of two parallel conducting plates at close distance due to the vacuum fluctuation of the electromagnetic field. Its derivation can be found in many introductory works on quantum optics. Here we return to the original paper by Casimir and find subtle nuances in his derivation that are worth discussing to give a complete picture of a mathematically sound derivation of the effect.
tldr: The paper revisits Casimir's original derivation of the Casimir effect, discussing mathematical nuances for a sound derivation.
motivation: To clarify subtle points in Casimir's original derivation that are often glossed over in textbooks.
method: The authors analyze Casimir's original paper step-by-step, identifying and addressing mathematical gaps.
result: A mathematically rigorous derivation of the Casimir effect is presented, with careful handling of regularization and boundary conditions.
conclusion: The Casimir effect derivation can be made fully rigorous by addressing subtle mathematical issues, confirming the physical result.

title: Refractive Indices Of Y$_2$SiO$_5$ In The Near-infrared
authors: Shijun Zhang, J\'er\^ome Debray, Beno\^it Boulanger, Pierre Lemonde, Thierry Chaneli\`ere
abstract: ArXiv:2606.26971v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Y[MATH]SiO[MATH] is a reference birefringent material for optical quantum technologies. The refractive index is primarily known in the visible spectrum, whereas this crystal is also used in the near-infrared. We begin by analysing historical measurements, as well as the modelling proposed at the time. The absence of refractive index tabulated values in the near- and mid-infrared ranges motivated us to carry out independent measurements.
